source.title: Grow Your Faith Daily
source.attribution: A Reborn guide in our own words, drawing on The Navigators, the University of Notre Dame's McGrath Institute for Church Life and the Greater Good Science Center.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. Scripture is referenced by book and chapter only, with no quotations. References: The Navigators, How to have a daily quiet time, https://www.navigators.org/resource/how-to-have-a-daily-quiet-time/; McGrath Institute for Church Life, University of Notre Dame, How to practice lectio divina, https://mcgrathblog.nd.edu/how-to-practice-lectio-divina-praying-with-scripture; Wikipedia, Lectio Divina, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lectio_Divina; Wikipedia, Sabbath in Christianity, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabbath_in_Christianity; Greater Good Science Center, What is forgiveness, https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/forgiveness/definition

cards.title: Faith grows like a friendship: through time spent together
cards.body:
For many believers, faith is not just a set of beliefs but a living relationship with God. And like any close relationship, it grows through regular, honest time together, not just occasional big moments.

This guide offers a simple daily rhythm: setting aside time and place, praying, reading scripture slowly, reflecting, giving thanks, worshipping, and living your faith with others. It is written mainly from a Christian perspective, but people of many traditions may find ideas here that help.

There is no need to be perfect. Small, steady steps matter more than dramatic efforts. Think of it as showing up each day with an open heart, trusting that growth often happens quietly, like a seed in the soil.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself honestly: what would a closer walk with God look like for me this year? Write one sentence.

quiz.question: According to this guide, what helps faith grow most?
options: Rare, dramatic spiritual experiences
Knowing all the right answers first
Regular, honest time with God, even in small steps
quiz.explanation: Like a friendship, faith deepens through steady, everyday time together rather than occasional big efforts.

cards.title: Set a regular time and place to meet with God
cards.body:
A daily time with God, often called a quiet time or devotion, is easier to keep when it has a fixed place in your day. Many people choose early morning before the house wakes up. Others prefer lunchtime or the evening. Pick the time when you're most likely to be alert and undisturbed.

Choose a spot too: a corner of your room, a chair by the window, even a parked car or a park bench. Keep your Bible, a notebook and a pen there.

Start small. Five to ten minutes a day is a wonderful beginning, and you can grow from there. Jesus himself often withdrew to quiet places to pray, as the Gospels describe in Mark 1.
cards.apply_it: Choose a time and place for a ten-minute quiet time and put your Bible and notebook there tonight.

quiz.question: What is a good way to begin a daily quiet time habit?
options: Start with five to ten minutes at a set time and place
Wait until you have free time
Start with two hours a day
Only do it on Sundays
quiz.explanation: A short, regular slot in a familiar place is easy to keep and can grow over time.

cards.title: Pray as an honest conversation, not a performance
cards.body:
Prayer is simply talking with God, and listening too. You don't need special words. God already knows your heart, so you can be completely honest about your joys, fears, anger and questions. The Psalms, such as Psalm 13 and Psalm 62, show people pouring out their real feelings.

If you're not sure where to start, a simple pattern can help. One well-known guide is ACTS: Adoration (praising God for who he is), Confession (owning what you've done wrong), Thanksgiving, and Supplication (asking for your needs and others'). The Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6 is another model.

Leave a little silence at the end. Prayer is a two-way relationship.
cards.apply_it: Today, pray using the four steps of ACTS, spending about one minute on each.

quiz.question: What does the A in the ACTS prayer pattern stand for?
options: Asking
Answers
Attendance
Adoration
quiz.explanation: ACTS stands for Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication.

cards.title: Read scripture slowly, letting a short passage speak to you
cards.body:
Reading the Bible isn't a race. Many believers grow most by reading a short passage slowly and letting it sink in, rather than rushing through chapters.

An ancient Christian practice called lectio divina, or sacred reading, offers a gentle pattern. Choose a few verses, for example from Psalm 23 or John 15. Read them slowly, ideally aloud, and notice a word or phrase that stands out. Read again and think about why it caught you. Read a third time and respond to God in prayer. Finally, rest quietly in his presence.

If you'd like more structure, a reading plan, such as one Gospel chapter a day, can guide you steadily through scripture.
cards.apply_it: Read Psalm 23 slowly three times today and write down the word or phrase that stands out most.

quiz.question: What is the heart of lectio divina?
options: Reading as many chapters as possible
Memorising the whole Bible
Slowly and prayerfully reading a short passage several times
Studying only ancient languages
quiz.explanation: Lectio divina invites you to read a short passage slowly, reflect, pray and rest in God's presence.

cards.title: Reflect and journal to apply what you read
cards.body:
Writing helps you slow down and notice what God may be teaching you. Keep a simple notebook for your quiet times.

After reading, try three questions. What does this passage say? What does it show me about God? What is one way I can live this out today? You might also note a verse that stood out, a prayer request, or something you're struggling with.

Over weeks and months, your journal becomes a record of your journey. Looking back, you'll often see prayers that were answered, lessons that took root, and ways you've grown that were invisible day to day. That can be a real encouragement during harder seasons.
cards.apply_it: After your next reading, write one line answering: 'One way I can live this out today is...'

quiz.question: Which is a helpful journaling question after reading scripture?
options: What is one way I can live this out today?
How many pages did I read?
Did anyone see me reading?
quiz.explanation: Asking how to apply a passage helps faith move from reading into daily life.

cards.title: Memorise a verse so it stays with you all day
cards.body:
When you memorise scripture, you carry it with you into work, school and difficult moments. Many believers find that a verse learned by heart comes back to mind just when they need comfort, courage or wisdom. Psalm 119 speaks of hiding God's word in the heart.

Start with one short verse a week. Write it on a card or set it as your phone background. Say it aloud several times a day, especially at set moments like brushing your teeth or waiting for a bus. Test yourself by covering the words and reciting from memory.

Good verses to begin with might come from Philippians 4, Joshua 1 or Proverbs 3.
cards.apply_it: Choose one short verse today, write it on a card, and say it aloud three times before bed.

quiz.question: Which is a practical way to memorise a verse?
options: Read it once and hope it sticks
Write it down and recite it several times a day
Only read it on Sundays
quiz.explanation: Seeing and saying a verse often, then testing yourself, helps it stay in your memory.

cards.title: Practise gratitude and worship throughout the day
cards.body:
Gratitude turns our attention to God's goodness, even on hard days. Scripture often encourages giving thanks in all circumstances, as in 1 Thessalonians 5. Try noticing three gifts each day, such as a meal, a kind word or a safe journey, and thanking God for them.

Worship isn't only singing in church, though music is a beautiful part of it. It can be a song you play on the way to work, a quiet word of praise while you walk, or doing your work well as an offering. Colossians 3 encourages doing everything as if for the Lord.

Small moments of thanks and praise, scattered through the day, keep your heart turned towards God.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, write down three things from today you're thankful for and thank God for each one.

quiz.question: According to this guide, worship can include...
options: Songs, quiet praise and doing everyday work as an offering
Only formal singing in a church building
Only prayers said by a leader
quiz.explanation: Worship can fill everyday life, from singing to quiet praise to how you do your work.

cards.title: Grow alongside others in community and fellowship
cards.body:
Faith was never meant to be lived alone. From the early church in Acts 2, believers met together to learn, pray, share meals and support one another. Hebrews 10 encourages Christians not to give up meeting together.

A local church or fellowship gives you worship, teaching, encouragement and people who will pray for you. A small group or Bible study lets you ask questions honestly and be known. Having one or two trusted friends who check in on your spiritual life can make a huge difference.

If you're new or nervous, start small: attend one service, introduce yourself to one person, or join one group. Belonging often grows slowly, over weeks.
cards.apply_it: This week, reach out to one believer you trust and suggest praying together or meeting to talk about faith.

quiz.question: Why does community matter for faith?
options: Others encourage, teach and pray for you as you grow
It replaces the need for personal prayer
It is only for church leaders
It matters only at weddings and funerals
quiz.explanation: Fellowship provides support, accountability and shared worship that help faith grow.

cards.title: Live out your faith by serving others
cards.body:
Faith grows not only in quiet moments but in action. Jesus taught that caring for the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the lonely is a way of serving him, as described in Matthew 25. James 2 reminds believers that faith shows itself in what we do.

Service can be small and daily: helping a neighbour carry shopping, visiting someone who is lonely, cooking for a family in need, or volunteering at your church or a local charity. It can also be how you treat people at home and at work, with patience, honesty and kindness.

Serving others takes the focus off ourselves and often brings deep joy and a sense of purpose.
cards.apply_it: Do one quiet act of kindness for someone today without telling anyone about it.

quiz.question: Which is an example of serving others in daily life?
options: Only giving large donations
Telling everyone about your good deeds
Visiting a lonely neighbour or helping someone in need
Waiting for a formal role at church
quiz.explanation: Everyday acts of care and kindness are a real and powerful way to live out faith.

cards.title: Receive forgiveness and offer it to others
cards.body:
At the centre of the Christian faith is grace: God's forgiveness, freely offered. When you fall short, you don't need to hide or punish yourself. You can confess honestly and receive forgiveness, as 1 John 1 encourages, then begin again.

Forgiven people are also called to forgive. Jesus's teaching in Matthew 18 and the Lord's Prayer link the two closely. Forgiving someone doesn't mean pretending they did no harm, excusing it, or always trusting them again. It means releasing the desire for revenge and handing the hurt to God.

Forgiveness is often a process, not a single moment. You can pray for the willingness to forgive even before you feel it.
cards.apply_it: Bring one hurt you're carrying to God in prayer today and ask for help to begin letting it go.

quiz.question: What does forgiving someone NOT require?
options: Releasing the desire for revenge
Pretending the harm never happened or excusing it
Bringing the hurt to God
quiz.explanation: Forgiveness lets go of revenge but does not deny the harm or demand instant trust.

cards.title: Keep going through dry seasons and doubts
cards.body:
Every believer goes through times when prayer feels empty, the Bible seems flat and God feels far away. Doubts and questions come too. This is a normal part of faith, not a sign that you've failed. Many people in scripture, from the writers of Psalm 42 and Psalm 88 to Elijah in 1 Kings 19, knew these seasons.

In dry times, keep showing up in small ways, even if it's just a short honest prayer. Be truthful with God about how you feel. Rest, eat well and sleep, as Elijah did.

Talk to a trusted pastor, mentor or friend about your questions. Honest searching can lead to a deeper, more mature faith.
cards.apply_it: If faith feels dry right now, tell God honestly how you feel in one short prayer, and share it with one trusted person.

quiz.question: What does this guide suggest during a spiritually dry season?
options: Hide your doubts from everyone
Give up until feelings return
Pretend everything is fine
Keep showing up honestly and talk with someone you trust
quiz.explanation: Dry seasons are normal; honest prayer, small steady habits and wise support help you through.

cards.title: Make room for rest and a weekly sabbath
cards.body:
Rest is a gift woven into scripture from the very beginning. In Genesis 2, God rests on the seventh day, and the commandment in Exodus 20 calls people to keep a weekly day holy. Jesus invites the weary to come to him for rest, as recorded in Matthew 11.

Christians observe this in different ways, but the heart of it is the same: one day in seven to stop working, worship, enjoy God's goodness and spend time with people you love. It reminds us that our worth doesn't come from how much we produce.

Plan ahead so you can truly rest: finish chores beforehand, put work aside, and fill the day with worship, nature, family and joy.
cards.apply_it: Choose part of one day this week to set aside work and screens for worship, rest and time with loved ones.

quiz.question: What is the heart of a weekly sabbath?
options: Catching up on all your work
Stopping work to worship, rest and enjoy God's goodness
Following a long list of strict rules
Avoiding other people
quiz.explanation: Sabbath is a regular rhythm of rest and worship that reminds us our worth isn't based on productivity.
